items.action: Barcos d'água acima carried goods between the Ribatejo and Lisboa, sailing down and up the Tejo, taking produce to the capital and bringing back goods.
Trains, then lorries and trucks, offered faster and cheaper freight transport, so the old sailing boats gradually stopped trading.
Ports grew along both banks at points of heavy traffic, where goods gathered for boats to collect and where arriving cargo was unloaded.

items.action: A medium-sized boat could then sail upriver to Vila Velha or beyond, in a Tejo without dams, with abundant free-flowing water and no silting.
items.conditions: no dams, abundant water, no silting

items.action: Philip II of Spain, ruling Portugal, tried to make the Tejo navigable at least to Toledo, with some successful initiatives.
The Chamusca ports saw major freight movement, about 5,500 tonnes passing through, counting goods leaving and arriving.
items.conditions: outgoing goods were more than incoming

items.action: Barcos d'água acima were shallow medium-sized boats with a tall mast raked aft, a large triangular bastardo sail and a small foresail.
items.conditions: 1 to 2 m of water enough, even in midsummer
items.gear: mast, bastardo sail, small bow sail

items.action: Crew roles: the arrais, often the owner, commanded and steered; experienced camaradas worked the boat; young moços learned the trade.
Because they suited calm river waters, these boats were authorised to sail only upriver, not at sea beyond the bar.
items.conditions: only água acima, not the sea

items.action: The run to Lisboa carried wine, cork, coal, cereals, olive oil, straw, firewood and fruit; the return brought salt, manufactured goods, fertiliser and news.
